Fort William First Nation

Fort William First Nation is an Anishinaabe community connected to the western end of Lake Superior and Anemki-Wajiw. These starting sources pair historical treaty interpretation with a named Elder’s account of family, land-based learning and education.

Read the sources [1] Thunder Bay Museum [2] Anishinabek News

01

Treaty history in a particular community

Thunder Bay Museum’s Robinson-Superior account connects Fort William First Nation with the1850 treaty and identifies Anemki-Wajiw as Mount McKay. Its archival caption describes an annuity gathering there in1933. These records offer a way to study the treaty relationship through a named community and documented event, rather than treating every north-shore First Nation as interchangeable. The museum’s interpretation does not settle present legal rights or establish that treaty commitments were fulfilled.

Read the sources [1] Thunder Bay Museum

02

An Elder’s experience of learning

In Rick Garrick’s2021 report, Fort William Elder Rita Fenton recalls a childhood in which her family hunted, fished and gathered from the land. She also describes later education and renewed learning about Indigenous histories. Her public storytelling connects personal experience with responsibilities to younger generations. This is an attributed individual life account; it should not stand in for every Fort William family or authorize reproducing cultural teachings beyond their public context.

Read the sources [2] Anishinabek News
